However, the literature also does not state that secondary stress is absent.'
318.quote: Full length occurs in the penultimate syllable of a word pronounced in isolation or at the end of a sentence.... This constitutes the characteristic penultimate accent of Tswana.... When a word is in non-final sentence position, it still retains its penultimate accent, but in much lesser degree, i.e. only half-length is used. Normal short length occurs in final and non-penultimate syllables, and in some monosyllabic words.
318.loc: Cole 1955 p. 55, quoted on Hyman 2009 p. 198, sec. 2 'Bantu penultimate lengthening: an overview'; Coetzee 2001 p. 7 (sec. 4); Bennett et al. 2016 p. 244, 'Penultimate lengthening'
318.idn: Tswana (Coetzee 2001; Cole 1955 as cited); 'South African Setswana varieties' -- speakers from Taung (North-West province), Kuruman and Kimberley (Bennett et al. 2016); Tswana, first-year students at North-West University, Potchefstroom (Schubö et al. 2021); data: Coetzee 2001: data from published sources only…
318.exq_: The penultimate syllable of a prosodic phrase is normally lengthened (Cole 1955: 55, University of Botswana 2001: 31, IPA 2010: 349). These lengthened syllables are also sometimes described as stressed (University of Botswana 2001: 32). [Bennett et al. 2016: 244]
318.tone: Two phonemic tones, high and low; 'tonal processes can cause high and low tones to manifest on the same syllable, resulting in a surface rising or falling tone' (Bennett et al. 2016: 243). The penultimate prominence is realised as vowel/syllabic-sonorant length ('penultimate accent', Cole 1955: 55), independent of lexical tone; vowel length is otherwise not phonemic (Schuboe et al. 2021: 20).

SUPPLEMENTARY for nominal/derivational categories: Creissels 2020 'Grammaticalization in Tswana' (in Bisang & Malchukov eds., De Gruyter, 769-801); Creissels 'Number in Tswana' (in Acquaviva & Daniel eds., De Gruyter, 107-127); Creissels 'Applicative…
morph.rootq: Creissels describes word prominence purely positionally, as prepausal penultimate lengthening with no reference to root or stem: 'the lengthening that affects the penultimate syllable of words in immediate prepausal position is noted explicitly' (ApplTswana fn., p.2); 'the postlexical rules that operate in prepausal position, according to which, (a) the penultimate syllable is lengthened, (b) if the tone of the penultimate syllable is H, it surfaces as a HL falling tone, and (c) a final H immediately preceded by another H (realized as HL) surfaces as L' (Creissels 2017 cj/dj §4.1); 'the rule of prepausal penultimate lengthening and a tonal rule that converts H H and H L sequences…
morph.elicq: 'Tswana words are quoted with a phonetic transcription of their pronunciation in contexts that trigger the application of no post-lexical tone rule ... This quotation form is different from the transcription of their pronunciation in isolation, which can be deduced from this quotation form by applying the rule of prepausal penultimate lengthening ... For example, the pronunciation of mang [máŋ́] “who?” and ope [ʊ́pɛ́] “nobody” in isolation is [mâːŋ̀] and [ʊ̂ːpɛ̀], but [máŋ́] and [ʊ́pɛ́] in non-prepausal contexts.' (Creissels 2014 fn.4 p.3-4); 'All the examples are given with their usual notation in current Tswana orthography, and with a phonetic transcription reflecting the pronunciation…
morph.stmt: Creissels: 'Typologically, Tswana is in almost every respect a typical Bantu language': nouns carry obligatory gender-number PREFIXES ('many morphemes that are unquestionably prefixes (in particular, subject indexes and object indexes) are written as if they were separate words'), while 'A Tswana verb form consists of a root (irreducible lexical element) together with an obligatory suffix (the final vowel, or simply final) and a variable number of other affixes', the template running from position –4 (negation) through –3 (subject index), –2 (TAM/NEG), –1 (object indexes/reflexive) before the root to +1 (valency suffixes), +2 (perfect), +3 (passive), +4 (final vowel), +5…

tn.quote: Setswana has two phonemic tones, high and low. The tonal phonology of Setswana is quite complex, and tonal processes can cause high and low tones to manifest on the same syllable, resulting in a surface rising or falling tone (see Jones 1928 and Chebanne et al. 1997 for much more detailed discussion of tone patterns). Some examples of lexical tone distinctions are given in (3). ... Penultimate lengthening The penultimate syllable of a prosodic phrase is normally lengthened ... These lengthened syllables are also sometimes described as stressed (University of Botswana 2001: 32).

In some styles of speech, the physical realization of accent is a quite noticeable prolongation of the vowel of the syllable. ... This means that it is the syllable before /-nyi/ that gets the penultimate accent (Unit 1, Note 1). 319.idn: Shona (Rhodesia; standardized Shona based on Zezuru, Manyika, Korekore), as spoken by two individuals with emendations toward the more central dialects; transcription shows a 'relatively central' and an 'eastern' tone system simultaneously (Unit 1 Note 2, pp. 5-6). The two scan-garbled words before 'of Shona' in the…
319.exq_: The accent generally falls on the next to last syllable before a pause.
319.tone: Tone language: two tones, high and low ('All of the levels may be summarized in terms of two entities, which will be called tones'); pitch alone distinguishes words (nhanga 'pumpkin' vs nhanga 'yard'; kuchera 'to dig' vs 'to draw [water]') and grammatical functions. Accent (extra force + duration on the next-to-last syllable before a pause) is described separately from tone and may fall on a low or a high syllable (Stevick 1965, Unit 1 Notes 1-2, pp. 4-5).

This means that it is the syllable before /--nyi/ that gets the penultimate accent.' morph.elicq: Stevick 1965 p.4: 'In the sentences of the basic dialogue, certain syllables will strike the student's ear as being more prominent than others. ... Compare the sentences: Mwarara here? Ndarara zvangu. ... The accent generally falls on the next to last syllable before a pause. ... The student should notice whether this is true of his own tutor.' morph.stmt: Zentz 2016 pp.15-17: 'Shona verbs are highly agglutinative... The verb root obligatorily takes a suffix called the final vowel, but in between, it may take one or more suffixes (traditionally called extensions in the Bantuist literature) that often change the valency of the root.... The stem is required to take a subject marker prefix... If there is an object marker, that is closest to the stem, then tense/aspect prefixes, then the subject marker prefix, and then negation or the relative marker'; Fivaz & Ratzlaff 1972 p.9: 'Every noun in Shona has one of these class prefixes and a stem' -- i.e. inflection (noun class/number, locative, agreement, subject, object, tense-aspect, negation)…

corr.head: StressTyp2's coding does not match the source
corr.detail: In even-length words the database's coded patterns drop the clash between the odd-numbered-syllable stresses and the final-syllable stress, but every source keeps it (Miller 1996:698 transcribes a four-syllable word as "1022", i.e. primary stress on the first syllable and secondary on both the third and fourth; Gordon puts the language in his binary-plus-clash class).

320.dq: Miller describes the basic stress pattern as alternating, with primary stress on the initial syllable, and an apparently optional pattern of clash tolerance by stressing the final syllable (19a–c). (19) a. "kin.ka 'onion' 12 b. "hi.pik.ka 'drank' 102 c. "nim.mi.man.tin 'one of us' 1022 (Miller 1996:698) ... Unstressed vowels in the final syllable are devoiced (Miller 1996:697–698).
320.dloc: van Urk, Clash tolerance (MIT generals ms.) §2.2.2
320.srule: Secondary stress on odd-numbered syllables counting from the left after the initial primary (moras rather than syllables per Gordon 2002 fn. 39 and Elzinga 1999); Miller 1996:698 (via van Urk sec. 2.2.2 and StressTyp2 'alternating from the first syllable, 1R') additionally stresses the final syllable, giving a clash in even-length words (kin.ka 12, nim.mi.man.tin 1022) -- a final stress van Urk calls 'apparently optional'; Elzinga 1999 states only the odd-mora alternation (no separate final stress).

morph.stmt: Predominantly suffixing with a closed set of verbal prefixes: "verbs often have prefixes indicating grammatical voice and the type of instrument with which the action is done. They also often have one or more suffixes indicating directional and adverbial notions as well as tense and aspect" (Crum, Crum & Dayley 2001:10); "nearly all the overt grammatical markers occur in the verb phrase. The only system of grammatical markers in the noun phrase is the subject-object-possessive case markers" (Tanner 1970:4), with case, number, tense-aspect, subordination, benefactive/causative -nkɨ, nominalizers and verbalizers all suffixal, and only reflexive/reciprocal na-/nɨɨ-, intransitivizing te- and…

321.dq: 5.2.2 Primary stress always occurs on the penultimate syllable of words having two or more syllables. || 5.2.3 Words having two and three syllables carry only primary stress. || 5.2.4 Words having only four syllables carry a single secondary stress on the first syllable.

321.prule: Primary stress always falls on the penultimate syllable of words of two or more syllables (it moves rightward to stay penultimate under suffixation; prefixes do not affect it); one-syllable words other than particles carry primary stress, and particles are stressless.
321.srule: Allison 1979: words of two and three syllables carry primary stress only; words of four syllables, and unprefixed words of more than four syllables, carry one secondary stress on the first syllable. In prefixed words of more than four syllables the secondary stress is perturbed by the prefix (a one-syllable prefix makes it fluctuate between the first and second syllables; a two-syllable prefix carries obligatory secondary stress on its own first syllable, the stem's secondary being retained); primary stress is never affected.
321.quote: 5.2 Stress. The accentual system consists of two stress levels, primary ['] and secondary ["], both of which are readily predictable. ... 5.2.2 Primary stress always occurs on the penultimate syllable of words having two or more syllables. ... 5.2.3 Words having two and three syllables carry only primary stress. ... 5.2.4 Words having only four syllables carry a single secondary stress on the first syllable, in addition to the primary word stress. ... 5.2.5.1 Unprefixed words having more than four syllables carry a single secondary stress on the first syllable, in addition to the primary word…

322.quote: The distribution of this pattern in Austronesian, however, is not simple. In addition to the languages just mentioned, final syllable prominence is also found in western and northern Borneo, e.g. Salako (Adelaar 2005:21), Bidayuh (Rensch 2006:48-49), Begak (Goudswaard 2005:35), as well as Sumatra, e.g. Sikule (Kähler 1955), Gayo (Eades 2005:31), Besemah (McDonnell 2014), Lampung (Walker 1975) but exceptions abound. For instance, two languages of the Barrier Islands, Nias and Mentawai have penultimate prominence despite being located on the far western Rim of the Austronesian area.

corr.head: StressTyp2's coding does not match the source
corr.detail: The grammar StressTyp2 itself cites (Tauberschmidt 1999:10-11) gives initial stress only in words of one to three syllables, and stress on the first and penultimate syllables in words of four or more (five syllables = 10010). The coding of stress on every odd-numbered syllable overgeneralizes from four-syllable words, where first-plus-penultimate happens to coincide with the odd-numbered syllables.

Basic stress patterns include: (1) Stress on word initial syllable followed by unstressed syllable or word juncture ... (2) Double-syllable stress ... (3) Double-syllable non-stress in limited occurrence ... He…
324.prule: None ridable. The primary of record describes three coexisting word-level basic patterns, lexically distributed: at length 1, 1; at length 2, 10 / 11 / 00 (00 "in limited occurrence"); at length 3, 100 / 110. No single quantity-insensitive count-computable pattern per length exists; StressTyp2's exhaustive-initial coding (10, 100, 1000...) contradicts its own cited primary.
324.srule: Wheeler & Wheeler 1962 rank no word stress as secondary: their 'two degrees' are ordinary stress and heavy stress /˝/, the latter marking phrase-group peak syllables (§2 p. 103, §5 p. 108); some words carry two equal stresses ('double-syllable stress': /ʔę́ká/ 'firewood', /yúyúp'ɨ/ 'termite nest') and a few none (/yɨʔɨ/ 'I'), lexically. Superseding statement, Wheeler 1987 I §2.2.3-2.2.3.2 (pp. 89-91): the non-final syllables of the base bear secondary stress ('acento secundario de la forma básica'); after the base, suffixes and enclitics alternate unstressed-stressed-unstressed-stressed counting from the first suffix (yó-gu-té; yó-daʔ-kú-di-té = 1-0-1-0-1), a few inherently stressed suffixes (-máʔi NEG, -déʔá IRR) giving adjacent stresses.
324.quote: Phonemic stress is present in two degrees within the word, which is defined as the minimum elicitable form or such a minimum form expanded by following unstressed syllables. Although no very good minimal contrasts have been found, stress is a conditioning factor ... Basic stress patterns include: (1) Stress on word initial syllable ... (2) Double-syllable stress ... (3) Double-syllable non-stress

324.cfw: Wheeler & Wheeler 1962 describe Siona stress as phonemic with a basic initial pattern while admitting no good minimal pairs, but Wheeler's fuller grammars (1970, 1987) call stress non-contrastive and predictable from the base, with every base syllable stressed and the strongest stress on the base's second or final syllable, and Bruil 2014 finds no contrastive stress at all in Ecuadorian Siona, so the later reference grammar outweighs the early sketch even though all three Wheeler works come from one fieldworker.

325.srule: No rhythmic secondary stress described. Gasparini names one 'accent secondaire', realized as vowel length: in six derived verbs (of 68 long-vowel tokens) the root's long vowel keeps its length, with a pitch rise, while the intensity accent falls on the penult of the derived word, e.g. [uːkʷakéɾa] < [úːkʷa] 'passer'; 'si l'accent tonique se déplace dans un cas de suffixation, la longueur vocalique reste fixe'.

evidence_works.detail: Sec. 5.1.1 'Variaciones de acento' (pp. 360-361) sorts the unstressed enclitics into two classes: those that leave the host's stress where it is (nominalizers 2 he and 3 hi, particle 6 čõ Cualitativa, particle 4 rã Identificación, the 'funciones') and those that shift it (particle 7 čɨ̃ Indicador de interés, particle 8 sa Indicador de locación, particle 9 te Enfático, particle 10 allomorph Yã Negativo, temporal 4 re, nominalizer 1 sa): 'Cada una de estas enclíticas foneticamente se funde con la palabra precedente quedando el acento en la penúltima sílaba de la palabra fonética' (p. 361). Sec. 1.3 (p. 286) adds that the last stressed syllable of a sentence 'puede ser cualquiera de las cinco últimas sílabas de la oración', i.e. up to four unstressed syllables can follow the last stress. This is the phonological-word domain of the penult rule stated over clitic attachment; it agrees with the catalog's penult rule and its WORD domain and adds which enclitics count inside that word.

evidence_works.work: Crothers, Lorentz, Sherman & Vihman (eds.) 1979, Handbook of phonological data from a sample of the world's languages: A report of the Stanford Phonology Archive (Stanford University vol. 1: 497-498, entry 965 Sirionó), quoting Priest 1968, Phonemes of the Sirionó language (Linguistics 41: 102-108)
evidence_works.detail: The SPA entry (p. 497) quotes Priest 1968 p. 102: 'The stress group consists of a sequence of from one to four syllables with one primary stress. Stress is phonemic. It usually occurs on the penultimate syllable.' and glosses the residue as 'The only exception is certain words that end in particular vowel sequences' (p. 102). It also records Priest's two counting conventions that make the penult rule hold: 'Each long vowel is interpreted as two like phonemes because (1) there are frequent vowel clusters in the language, and (2) this interpretation best coincides with the predominant stress pattern.' (p. 105) and that unstressed intervocalic / initial prevocalic [i] [u] are taken as /yod/ /w/ because 'This interpretation results in the fewest possible exceptions to the predominant stress pattern.' (p. 105).

sources.text: "Stress is grammatically predictable and is not written. Primary stress occurs on the stem, and if there is a multi-syllable stem, on its second syllable. Reduplicated stems take this stress on the repetition. There are a few exceptions to this rule which are as follows: (1) Compound words take primary stress on the initial root. (2) Pronouns and the irregular verb 'give' take primary stress on the final syllable. (3) Exclamations take primary stress on the initial syllable. (4) Zero class verbs take primary stress on the first order suffix." (Wells 1979:5)

morph.stmt: Siroi is almost exclusively suffixing: verbs are 'inflected for tense, number and person' by suffixes ('The endocentre consists of the obligatory stem and the first order affixes [class-marker or object suffix]... The exocentre consists of dependent and independent suffixes which follow the verb endocentre', §2.2 p.27), non-verbs are classified by 'suffixation versus non-suffixation' and take only enclitics (-nge, -nu, -ok) and postposed particles (§2.1 p.12); the sole prefix in the grammar is the 'Causal Prefix te-... kile-' on some semi-transitive verbs (§2.2.1.2 p.28), beside an object-plural infix -g- and widespread full reduplication.

contra.head: StressTyp2's coding depends on which source is followed
contra.detail: The database's quoted passage from Dogil says "Sources differ" on whether a final odd-numbered syllable is stressed, and the database codes both variants; a third, orthoepic tradition with secondary stress fixed on the penultimate syllable (Mocová 2012) would remove even the tied-output coverage our census gives the pattern.

327.dq: The stress rule operates on prosodic words as a whole, so affixes are stress-sensitive.

327.srule: Secondary stresses alternate on odd-numbered syllables after the initial main stress (ˈnepoˌveziem 'I will not carry'); sources differ as to whether a final odd-numbered syllable gets secondary stress (ˈnepoˌvezieˌme or ˈnepoˌvezieme 'we will not carry'); StressTyp2's summary pattern codes no secondary stress on the final syllable.
327.quote: Slovak has a quantity insensitive system with main stress on the initial syllable. Secondary stresses form an alternating pattern with higher prominence on odd-numbered syllables counting from the right. Sources differ as to whether or not a final odd-numbered syllable gets secondary stress. (Dogil forthc.)

morph.rootq: Hanulíková & Hamann 2010 (JIPA 40:376): 'Primary stress is always on the first syllable of the phonological word. Prepositions are integrated into the phonological word, and therefore attract stress if they contain a vowel (e.g. na stole [ˈnastɔlɛ] ‘on the table’). Eastern dialects have penultimate stress due to Polish influence.' — the domain is the phonological word (prefixes ne-, na-, roz- etc. and even proclitic prepositions take the stress), not the root. Same in Czambel 1902 p.194: 'prízvuk slova pošmykuje sa na predložku, nakoľko je táto jednoslabičná. Vyslovujeme totiž pred-dom, po-dom, na-dom atp.; s prízvukom na predložke.' MSJ 1966 (morphology volume) has no stress chapter.
morph.elicq: Hanulíková & Hamann 2010:373: 'The transcriptions of the wordlists and of the short text are based on recordings of a female Slovak native speaker (aged 28 years) from Bratislava who speaks what is considered Standard Slovak. The remaining examples are spoken by a female speaker (aged 32 years) from Košice who also speaks Standard Slovak.' (recorded wordlists plus the connected passage 'The North Wind and the Sun', whose transcription pp.377-378 marks initial stress on every phonological word; the stress statement itself is given without instrumental measurement.)
morph.stmt: MSJ 1966 p.51: 'Slovenská morfologická stavba je výrazne flektívna, pričom flektívny typ je najvýznamnejší v oblasti skloňovania' [Slovak morphological structure is markedly flective, the flective type being most important in declension] — all nominal and verbal inflection is by endings ('pádové prípony', 'osobné prípony', p.51, p.464: the grammatical morpheme of simple verb forms 'má podobu afixu-prípony'), while prefixes are confined to verbal aspect/Aktionsart ('Prefixácia je postup perfektivizácie...; sufixácia je postup imperfektivizácie', p.413), the po- future of motion verbs (p.479) and the negative ne- (p.471): a predominantly suffixing language with a productive layer of verbal…

327.sec_rule: None as a systemic feature: 'tzv. vedlajsi prizvuk v spisovnej slovencine neexistuje ako systemovy jav', ratio of stressed to unstressed syllables in the word 1: n-1 (Sabol 1986:394-395, on Petrekova's 1986 intensity measurements; restated Sabol 2015:258: non-initial syllables are only unstressed short/long). Competing descriptions to carry as variants: rhythmic secondary stresses on odd-numbered syllables counting from the left, sources differing on a final odd syllable, ˈnepoˌveziem, ˈnepoˌvezieˌme ~ ˈnepoˌvezieme (StressTyp2 < Dogil 1999); orthoepic norm: a weaker secondary on the 3rd syllable of 4-syllable words and the 3rd or penultimate syllable of longer words (Kral 1984:164 as quoted in Sabol 1986:394; penultimate in 5+-syllable words, Mocova 2012:37).
327.sec_quote: Secondary stresses form an alternating pattern with higher prominence on odd-numbered syllables counting from the right. tn.quote: Tónovou moduláciou sa nazývajú zmeny vo výške základného tónu reči. Tónovou moduláciou artikulačného prúdu vznikajú ďalšie suprasegmentálne javy: hlasový register a melódia. … S myšlienkovým a citovým obsahom vety súvisí melódia vety. Melódia je „pohyb, zmena a vlnenie tónovej zložky reči. Je to zmena výšky hlasu pri reči … V spisovnej slovenčine sa rozlišujú tri základné typy melódie: a) uspokojivá končiaca melódia (konkluzívna kadencia), b) neuspokojivá končiaca melódia (antikadencia), c) neuspokojivá nekončiaca melódia (semikadencia, polokadencia)“ (Kráľ, 1988, s. 172 – 174).
tn.translation: Tonal modulation is the term for changes in the height of the fundamental tone (pitch) of speech. Tonal modulation of the articulatory stream gives rise to further suprasegmental phenomena: voice register and melody. … The melody of the sentence is connected with the conceptual and emotional content of the sentence. Melody is 'the movement, change and undulation of the tonal component of speech. It is the change of voice pitch in speech … In Standard Slovak three basic types of melody are distinguished: a) satisfying terminal melody (conclusive cadence), b) unsatisfying terminal melody (anticadence), c) unsatisfying non-terminal melody (semicadence, half-cadence)' (Kráľ 1988: 172-174).
tn.cite: Sičáková, Ľuba. 2002. Fonetika a fonológia pre elementaristov. 1. vyd. Prešov: Náuka. 118 pp. ISBN 80-89038-15-8.
tn.locator: 'Tónová modulácia reči (hlasu)' / 'Melódia', pp. 97-98 (page numbers at page foot); function table Obr. 10 p. 88
tn.note: No lexical tone: pitch (tonal modulation) yields only voice register and sentence melody (three cadence types); of the suprasegmentals only quantity is marked distinctive, melody and stress are not.

327.cfw: Every source read puts Slovak main stress fixed on the first syllable of the word (Sabol 1986, Sabol & Zimmermann 1994, Kráľ 1984, Horák 1985, Benuš & Mády 2010, Mocová 2012, Dogil 1995 via StressTyp2); the sources differ only over secondary stress, which Sabol 1986 denies as a systemic feature while Kráľ 1984 places it on the third or penultimate syllable of longer words and Dogil's survey on alternating odd syllables, so the alternating pattern in the record's rule string is the one part not backed by the native literature.

329.srule: Not mentioned in Jacottet 1906:4 ('c) Syllables and Accent') or Tucker 1929 §§249-253 (pp. 99-100). [Dissenting analysis: Kunene 1961:165-167 §3.45, with main stress on the root syllable, gives one secondary stress on the penult in stems of four or more syllables and tertiary stress on the remaining syllables.]
329.quote: c) Syllables and Accent. All syllables end in a vowel, or in the nasal sound ng (at the end of a word), never in any consonantal sound. E. g.: mo-e-ti, traveller; ke noe-le, I have drunk; tsa-ma-eang, go away! m or n before a consonant forms a syllable by itself. E. g.: n-toa, war; le m-po-ne, you have seen me. The accent rests always on the penult, or on the last syllable when it ends in ng. E. g.: ho rata, to love; ratang, let you love; ntoa war; ntoeng, in the war.

morph.rootq: Jacottet 1906 p.4: 'The accent rests always on the penult, or on the last syllable when it ends in ng. E. g.: ho ráta, to love; ratáng, let you love; ńtoa, war; ntoéng, in the war.' The rule is stated over the word (penultimate syllable, with the syllabic-nasal/-ng proviso) with no reference to root or stem; the examples show the accent landing on suffixal material (ratáng with imperative-plural -ng, locative nto-éng) and on a prefixal syllabic nasal (ń-toa).
morph.elicq: Jacottet 1906 p.4 gives the rule with isolated citation forms only and says nothing about how it was established: 'All syllables end in a vowel, or in the nasal sound ng (at the end of a word) ... m or n before a consonant forms a syllable by itself. E. g.: n-toa, war; le m-po-ne, you have seen me. The accent rests always on the penult, or on the last syllable when it ends in ng. E. g.: ho ráta, to love; ratáng, let you love; ńtoa, war; ntoéng, in the war.' (pedagogical grammar by a long-resident missionary; no frame, text or instrumental evidence described).
morph.stmt: Jacottet 1906 pp.5-6: 'whereas in English as in other European languages grammatical inflections are marked by suffixes, they are in Sesuto marked by prefixes; the words change not at the end but at the beginning' (noun class/number, subject and object concords, reflexive, most TAM/negation markers precede the root), while derivation and part of inflection is suffixal: 'Most Sesuto verbs can form a certain number of Verbal derivative Species by means of different suffixes' (Lesson 36, p.147: causative -isa, applicative -ela, passive -o-/-w-, neuter -eha, reciprocal -ana, reversive -olla) plus perfect -ile, subjunctive/negative -e, imperative plural -ng, locative -ng and diminutive -ana…

tn.quote: From comparisons based on the inherent tone patterns of S. Sotho words, we come to the conclusion that there are two tonemes in this language, viz. a HIGH TONEME and a ... The low toneme comprises three variants or allotones, referred to here as mid (M), low (L), and low-minus (Lm) ... The high toneme ... apart from the fact that it may, like the low toneme, give rise to a falling glide in the penult, is a one-member toneme. ... S. 329.cfw: Jacottet 1906, Tucker 1929, Doke & Mofokeng 1957 (as quoted by Kunene 1961), Nussbaum & Lijane 1968 and the instrumental study of Mixdorff et al. 2011 all put the prominent syllable on the penult of a statement or isolated word, but Kunene 1961, a native speaker's phonology dissertation, denies that Southern Sotho is a stress language at all, treats the penultimate length as a phrase-level statement marker and places inherent main stress on the root syllable, so the penultimate reading is the clear majority view but not uncontested.

corr.head: Gordon (2002)'s coding does not match the source
corr.detail: For four-syllable words the database has stress only on the third syllable (0010), which deletes the main stress on the second syllable that all four primary sources assert. The correct pattern is either 0110 (second and third syllables both stressed, keeping the clash; this reading places the language in one of our census's pattern classes and is the one Hayes and Hyde favor) or 0100. The source may count moras rather than syllables.

330.heavy: A syllable with an organic long vowel or diphthong counts two moras (as does one with an inherent glottal stop); short vowels count one; syllable-final nasals add nothing.
330.dflt: second syllable when the first syllable is light (first syllable in light disyllables, whose final vowel is unvoiced)
330.srule: Stresses alternate by mora: every even-numbered mora is strong (relatively stressed), the second mora carrying the main stress; Sapir writes a grave accent for 'a secondary stress on a strong mora'. The final mora is always unvoiced, and Sapir states no penultimate secondary in even-mora words.

331.dq: In Sḵwx̱wú7mesh the first syllable of a morphologically simplex word is stressed if it contains a full vowel. The following bisyllabic words show that stress falls word initially.
331.dloc: Watt, Alford, Cameron-Turley, Gillon & Jacobs 2000:199 §1.2; fn.4 p.202 "these domains are completely isomorphic in Sḵwx̱wú7mesh"; StressTyp2 entry (Demers & Horn 1978:181) "Morphologically simple forms have penultimate stress" + words
331.heavy: full (non-schwa) vowel vs schwa: the leftmost full vowel takes primary stress; schwa is stressed only when the word has no full vowel (then the leftmost schwa). No role stated for vowel length or codas.
331.prule: Stress the leftmost full (non-schwa) vowel of a morphologically simplex word, or the leftmost schwa if there are no full vowels (full-vowel-initial bisyllables: initial; schwa+full bisyllables: final; all-schwa: initial; trisyllabic roots: initial primary). Strong (stress-attracting) suffixes such as -ullh 'young specimen', -alh 'times' take primary stress without exception, overriding the basic pattern and permitting adjacent stresses; weak suffixes and lexical suffixes -ach, -us follow the basic pattern.
331.srule: Secondary stress on alternating syllables counted from the primary (trochaic feet built left to right): trisyllabic roots initial primary + final secondary ([sxóxopìt] 'rabbit', [málalòs] 'raccoon'), four-syllable words predicted 1st primary + 3rd secondary; when a strong suffix takes the primary, the root syllable the basic rule selects keeps a secondary stress, even adjacent to the primary ([mèχaɬʔɔ́lɬ] 'cub', [sqʷəmày'ɔ́lɬ] 'puppy'). Dyck 2004:221, 229, 284 (Kuipers corpus): alternating binary rhythm confirmed but secondary stress 'does not surface consistently', appears mainly in polymorphemic words of 4+ syllables and not on the word-final syllable (final stresses are a present-day-speaker feature), and a trisyllabic root holds only one foot.

tn.quote: TONE. In monosyllabic terms a tonic accent is at times plainly discernible. It resembles one of the rising tones in Chinese. Father Morice has pointed out the same peculiarity in several of the dialects of the Déné. There, however, the function of tone is the same as in Chinese and marks a difference of meaning in words of the same form and sound; but in Sk·qō'mic this is not so. What purpose this tonic accent subserves in the Sk·qō'mic dialect is not at present clear to me.
tn.cite: Hill-Tout, Charles. 1900. Notes on the Sk'qō'mic of British Columbia, a Branch of the Great Salish Stock of North America. Report of the British Association for the Advancement of Science 70: 472-549.
tn.note: Rising 'tonic accent' heard on monosyllables but, unlike Chinese/Déné, said not to distinguish meaning; function unclear. Word accent contrastive (hair vs dog). p.504: superlative on a rising note.

331.cfw: Dyck 2004, the only book-length study of Squamish stress, and Demers & Horn 1978 both put default stress on the penultimate syllable when it holds a full vowel (or schwa plus resonant), as the record codes, while Bar-el & Watt 1998 and Watt et al. 2000 argue instead for the leftmost full vowel, a difference visible only in the rare simplex words of three or more syllables, where Dyck 2004 shows the initial-stressed examples are not roots. One further first-hand description conflicts (see the conflicting-description item); the entry follows Watt 2000.

336.dq: Stress is penultimate. Syllabic nasals may carry this penultimate stress. In some Arabic loans, stress is antepenultimate. (Ashton 1947:5)

336.srule: Only in compounds/close-knit groups: Polomé 1967 describes one word-stress per phonological word; a weaker, non-phonemic secondary stress falls on the penultimate of the FIRST constituent of a nominal compound (wataka kázi 'job-seekers', mwuza samáki 'fishmonger'), the word-stress on the penult of the second; inside the inflected verb Polomé also notes a secondary stress on the tense-marker when the relative applies to the infix (alichokivunja [aˌli-], n. 94 p. 191); no rhythmic/alternating secondary stress is described ('several non-phonemic degrees of loudness', unanalysed). [Later addition, Deen 2002:19 after Barrett-Keach 1986: in inflected verbs a secondary stress on the penultimate syllable counted from the right edge of the tense marker, Nì-me-fíka, Ni-mèsha-fíka, Ni-mekwìsha-fíka.]

morph.rootq: Main rule is purely word-based: 'Stress occurs as a rule on the penultimate vowel phoneme or syllabic allophone of a nasal phoneme. However, in some loanwords, mostly of Arabic origin, it is liable to occur on the antepenultimate' (Polome 1967 §2.1.5.1 p.50-51); 'Stress gives unity to the phonological word: as a consequence, such elements as the pronominal concord with the connective particle a ... or the invariable copulative ni or si ... are clitics, which belong phonologically with the following word' (p.51). But the grammar also states morpheme-specific stressability: 'Monosyllabic verbal stems show a morpheme (ku), which is usually considered as the prefix of the infinitive…
morph.elicq: No method is stated for the stress description itself. The only data statement is general (Preface p.ix): 'The Swahili material is based on the available current literature, grammatical descriptions and lexical data referred to in the bibliographical notes, as well as on personal field-notes gathered in Central and East Africa', with thanks to named Swahili speakers 'as well as the numerous school-teachers whose speech I taped during a research trip in East Africa.' The stress section argues from contrastive pairs and phrases (barabara 'exactly': barabara 'highway'; wataka kazi 'they want work': wataka kazi 'those looking for a job'; mzigo u mzito /umzito/), i.e. word- and phrase-level…
morph.stmt: Inflection is prefixal and derivation suffixal around the root: 'A Swahili verbal form is composed of various constituents which appear in a fixed order...: 1. preinitial; 2. initial; 3. postinitial; 4. marker; 5. infix; 6. root; 7. suffix(es); 8. final; 9. postfinal' (Polome 1967 §2.4.4 p.110), i.e. negation, subject, TAM, relative and object markers precede the root while derivational extensions (applicative, causative, passive, stative, reciprocal), the mood/negation final vowel and the plural/relative/interrogative postfinal clitics follow it; nouns and adjectives 'consist of a class-prefix plus a nominal stem' (§2.4.2.1 p.95) with number, diminutive and augmentative carried by the…

337.dq: The first syllable has the main stress, both in simple and in compound words.
337.dloc: Elmquist 1915:7 (archive.org); StressTyp2 entry (Bruce) weight window over the word stem
337.heavy: Bruce (via Frid, and StressTyp2 passage): a final or penult syllable that is 'closed (or otherwise heavy)' attracts stress; StressTyp2 note: 'Long vowels; closed syllables'. Frid's revision: superheavy finals (long V + C, or VCC, e.g. ba'na:n, kata'stro:f) take final stress, plain closed finals in trisyllables do not ('ma:raton vs re'aktor); 'a stressed syllable is always heavy' (bimoraic); final -el/-en/-er with schwa are never stressed. Frid p. 27: 'quantity sensitive (interacts with the weight of the rhyme of a syllable)'.
337.dflt: antepenult when final and penult are both open/light (Bruce); Frid's OT reanalysis treats penult as the general default
337.prule: Non-compound (monomorphemic) words: one stress inside a final three-syllable window - on the final syllable if it is closed/otherwise heavy (Frid: superheavy), else on the penult if it is closed/heavy, else on the antepenult when final and penult are both open (especially in hiatus); schwa finals -el/-en/-er never stressed; exceptions lexically prespecified. Frid's OT default is penultimate stress. Compounds and words with stress-bearing affixes: primary stress on the first stressable element.
337.srule: None in simplex (non-compound) words: 'The non-compound pattern is characterized by one stress (main stress)' (Bruce 1993:43; likewise Bruce 1999 via StressTyp2, Riad 2012:2-3 'there are no phonological secondary stresses in simplex words', Myrberg & Riad 2015:118); pre-stress syllables may be rhythmically strong but are unstressed. Secondary stress only in the compound pattern - true compounds, derivatives with stress-attracting affixes that keep root stress (hyper-, o-, -artad, -bar, -het, -dom, -skap) and formal compounds: main stress on the first stressable element, secondary stress on the last stressable element (root or stress-carrying affix), in Sweden Swedish always in the final element of a multi-member compound.
337.quote: The position of stress in Swedish words is not fixed, it can occur in different positions. This means that stress is distinctive, i.e., two words can differ only in their stress pattern. ... There is also a connection between stress and syllable weight: a stressed syllable is always heavy. Bruce 1993 summarises the most important rules for Swedish stress placement. A fundamental difference is made between monomorphemic and compound words (true compounds and derivatives). 4.1.1 Monomorphemic words. ... The following rules apply: • if the final syllable is closed (or otherwise heavy), stress is…
337.loc: Frid 2001 pp. 29-30, sec. 4.1 and 4.1.1; parametric summary p. 27 sec. 2.3.1; StressTyp2 entry (Bruce 1999, no page).
337.idn: Frid 2001 names the object only as 'Swedish' (lexical word stress in Swedish); the descriptive rule set it restates (Bruce 1993) is stated for 'Standard Swedish'; Riad 2012 (held, read) calls the same variety 'Central Swedish (roughly the standard language)'.
337.exq_: if the final syllable is closed (or otherwise heavy), stress is placed on this syllable. Exception: if the final syllable is -el, -en or -er ... there are several exceptions to this rule and it is easy to find counterexamples. ... exceptions have prespecified foot patterns in their input forms.

In loan-words and words ending in -eri the principal stress is generally placed on the last syllable'; §9.A.2: 'Strong secondary stress is also used in the terminations -dom, -het, -lek, -skap, -bar, -sam'; §281 Note 2 p.182: 'The prefixes be-, ent- and för- are unstressed and the Verb has Tone I... 337.sec_quote: The non-compound pattern is characterized by one stress (main stress), typically occurring on one of the three final syllables of a word stem. The compound pattern consists of two stresses: a main stress early in the word - in the 1st element of a compound (or equivalent word) - and a secondary stress late in the word - in the final element of a compound word.
337.sec_cite: Bruce, Gösta. 1993. On Swedish lexical stress patterns. Phonum 2: 41-50 (Umeå University, Dept. of Phonetics; open LUP scan, held, scan read) - the work Frid 2001 summarises; the same rule in Frid, Johan. 2001. Swedish word stress in optimality theory. Lund WPL 48: 25-40, sec. 4.1.3 p. 31 ('Compound words usually have two stresses, one on the first stressable element, and one on the second stressable element. The first one of these gets main stress, while the second gets secondary stress. Stressable elements are the root, and the affixes that carry stress.') and sec. 4.7 pp. 37-38 ('Main stress goes to the leftmost stressable element, while the last stressable element receives secondary stress. Other stresses (in compounds with more than two parts) are not realised'); and Bruce, G. 1999. 'Swedish'. In H. van der Hulst (ed.), Word Prosodic Systems in the Languages of Europe, ch. 8 - available only as StressTyp2 entry (held database): 'The non-compound stress pattern is characterized by having only one foot (and one stress) established within the three syllable window of the word. Possible preceding syllables which remain unfooted will typically be under the influence of post-lexical, phrasal rhythm rules.'

evidence_works.detail: In Stockholm Swedish news speech the accentual fall is significantly larger in Accent 2 than in Accent 1 words, and the phrase-level big-accent rise gets larger when a head beat accompanies the word and larger again with an added eyebrow beat, while the fall does not change with gestures. The paper takes Swedish as having lexical stress plus a privative Accent 1/Accent 2 tonal contrast on the stressed syllable, with compounds carrying a primary and a secondary stress, assigned Accent 2, and the big-accent H tone landing on the secondary stress.

evidence_works.detail: The article restates the Central Swedish system as a two-way tonal word accent (L* accent 1 vs H* accent 2) on the stressed syllable, distinctive in about 350 minimal pairs, assigned mainly by the suffix and by secondary stress (all compounds accent 2), with South Swedish the tonal mirror image; this agrees with the entry's tone-and-stress class and adds the assignment rules, the compound secondary-stress detail and the cited pitch-fall sizes. Its own contribution is neural (ERP/fMRI): accent 1, the accent with fewer lexical continuations, gives a larger pre-activation negativity than accent 2

tn.quote: The assignment of tone accent is partly lexical, partly intonational. ... Consider first the lexical distinction, which in Central Swedish amounts to a lexical H tone in accent 2 and no lexical tone in accent 1. ... 2sómmar is lexically marked for a lexical H tone, and 1bándy is not. Accent 2 is thus the marked member of a privative opposition, accent 1 being reducible to pure intonation. ... In lexically toneless forms (i.e. accent 1) there is no lexical tonal information to heed, only a stressed syllable, the TBU of all tonal association in Swedish.

tn.note: Privative tone accent: accent 2 = lexical H on the stressed syllable (from roots or posttonic suffixes), accent 1 toneless; one accent per prosodic word; stress separate; focal LH floats after H*.

337.cfw: Bruce 1993, Frid 2001 and 2003, Riad 2012 and Myrberg and Riad 2015 all state that Swedish main stress is not fixed but falls on a lexically or weight-determined syllable near the right edge of the stem (final heavy syllable, else heavy penult, else antepenult; initial only in compounds), and the fixed-initial coding rests only on Elmquist 1915 and the survey rows of Haugen 1976 and Gordon 2002, a view Bruce 1993 explicitly rejects as a prejudice based on the history of native vocabulary.

339.dq: Primary stress is generally on the penult of words without affixes spoken in isolation. When affixes are added new stress patterns occur. From these patterns Tacana words can be classified into three classes: 1. stress on the second syllable 2. stress on the third syllable 3. mixed. (Key 1968:29)

339.heavy: Bimoraic syllables = VV / CVV (a vowel plus a glide cluster, which Guillaume syllabifies as a complex nucleus: 'In my own work on Tacana and Reyesano, I have posited VV and CVV syllable structures', p. 7); a mora is a 'vowel or semi-vowel y [j]'. Monomoraic = V / CV. No closed (CVC) syllables figure in the description.
339.dflt: All-monomoraic words: third syllable from the left at >=4 syllables (0010, 00100, 001000), penult below that (10, 010).
339.prule: Stress the 3rd mora counting from the left edge of the prosodic word (morae = vowels and the semivowel y [j]; VV/CVV syllables count two) when the prosodic word has at least four morae; when it has fewer than four morae, stress the penultimate syllable. Hence 4-syllable CV.CV.CV.CV -> third syllable (tata=kwána) but VV.CV.CV.CV -> second syllable (yawíkwase). Stated as the 'basic rule' holding 'underlyingly' for 'most lexemes'; domain is the prosodic word including enclitics (=kwana, =sa).

ev.text: Stress in Shilha is a non-phonemic feature. The stress patterns may be summarized briefly by stating that primary or heavy stress occurs on the last vowel of the stem, provided that the word had no affixes after the stem. ... [fn.] It should be noted that the stress patterns referred to here apply only to utterances consisting of a single word. If the utterance contains more than one word, the stress is reduced slightly on all vowels except those in the final word. It can be said, therefore, that primary stress occurs only at the end of an utterance.

340.prule: Primary (heavy) stress falls on the last vowel of the stem when no suffix follows the stem. If a vowel-bearing suffix follows, the stem-final vowel and the suffix vowel each carry only medium (secondary) stress and no vowel in the word is heavy; vowel-bearing prefixes carry medium stress, with heavy stress on the stem-final vowel; the other stem vowels are unstressed. Stress is non-phonemic. These patterns are stated for one-word utterances; in longer utterances the stresses of non-final words are slightly reduced and primary stress occurs only at the end of the utterance (Applegate 1958:9, section 1.8 and fn. 1).
340.srule: Applegate 1958: medium ('secondary') stress placed by morphology - on the vowel of a vowel-bearing prefix, and, when a vowel-bearing affix follows the stem, on both the stem-final vowel and the affix vowel; other stem vowels unstressed; one-word utterances only. Revised by later instrumental work, which finds no word-level prominence asymmetries at all (Roettger 2017: 58; Roettger, Bruggeman & Grice 2015; Bruggeman 2020: 46).

340.exc_quote: The stress patterns may be summarized briefly by stating that primary or heavy stress occurs on the last vowel of the stem, provided that the word had no affixes after the stem.

340.sec_quote: If there is an affix after the stem, and this affix contains a vowel, there is secondary or medium stress on the last vowel of the stem and also on the vowel of the affix. Affixes occurring before the stem and containing a vowel have medium stress; and the final vowel of the stem has heavy stress. The other vowels of the stem have zero stress.

341.sec_rule: Only in compounds: two-stem compound words have a double stress, main stress word-final and an additional stress on the last syllable of the first component (се́рбача́, қа́дбала́нд); no secondary stress is described for simplex words (Arzumanov & Sanginov 1988 §20, pp. 126-128 read).
341.sec_quote: В составных словах, состоящих из двух основ, отмечается двойное ударение (основное и добавочное): основное на конце слова, а добавочное на последнем слоге первого компонента: се́рбача́ — многодетный, қа́дбала́нд — высокий, рослый.

secx.sec_quote_tr: In compound words consisting of two stems a double stress (main and additional) is noted: the main one at the end of the word, and the additional one on the last syllable of the first component: sérbachá 'having many children', qádbalánd 'tall, well-grown'.

tn.quote: The most prominent investigations on Tajik speech were conducted by Khaskashev (1983, 2001). In those works … he came to the conclusion that word stress in Tajik is mainly tonal. … The stressed syllable nuclei in Tajik in most cases are marked by pitch and intensity. The latter acts as a less stable feature of the stressed syllable and mostly corresponds to the pitch (Khaskashev 1972: 12–14). … 1. Tonal stress (pitch accent, based on F0) can be found in Mazandarani (Ivanov 2014), Persian (Ivanov 1972, 1996, Polyakov 1988, Silanteva 2022), and Tajik (Khaskashev 1972, 1983).
tn.cite: Ivanov, Vladimir B. & Liubov G. Silanteva. 2023. Research on word stress in Iranian languages by Soviet and Russian scholars. Russian Journal of Linguistics 27(2): 392-417. doi:10.22363/2687-0088-31015
tn.locator: p. 405, sec. 5.2 'Tajik', first paragraph and p. 412, sec. 6 item 1
tn.note: No lexical tone described; pitch (F0 rise) is the main acoustic correlate of word stress, intensity secondary, which the authors term 'tonal stress (pitch accent)' after Khaskashev's experiments.

However, there appear to be cases which do not conform to the above rules and further study of stress will be necessary. Tal stress is not indicated in this study.

morph.stmt: Utsumi 2013 §1: 'The Talaud language has a rich morphology in which affixes attached to the verbs are abundant... derivational affixes attached to Talaud verb bases can total seven or more.' Concretely the verb is predominantly prefixing/infixing (voice-tense ma-/na-, maN-/naN-, um- ~ -um-, ni- ~ -in-, CV i-, causative pa-, potentive ʔa-, aspectual ua-) with a single voice suffix -anna (GV) and imperative -e; nominal relations are marked by prenominal proclitic-like markers (i-, ni-/nu-, si-/su-) and pronominal possessors/the 1sg genitive actor and the completive are enclitics (=ku/=ʔu, =ne, =te/=ke).

sources.text: "I.4. Stress — Word stress in Tamazight is a non-contrastive feature. The occurence of word stress is predictable: primary stress falls on the last vowel of the word (i.e. /V/ or [e])." (p. 17). Continuation for phonemically vowelless words (p. 18): "The above statement applies to words that phonemically do not contain a vowel /V/. ... In these cases, word primary stress is on the [e] of the last syllable." Examples given include /adiniy/ 'I will say', /ndawa/ 'we cured', /tfafad/ 'you (s.) woke up', /isal/ 'he asked', all with final stress.

343.cfw: Abdel-Massih's 1971 reference grammar states that stress falls on the last vowel of the word, but all its examples are verbs, and the later metrical studies of Central Atlas varieties by Faizi (2011, 2017, building on Faizi 2002 for Goulmima and Hdouch 2010 for Ait Wirra) find weight-sensitive stress in nouns (the rightmost heavy syllable, otherwise the initial syllable) with final stress only in simple verbs, while Penchoen (1973) reports no word-level stress at all for Ayt Ndhir.

344.srule: Poppe 1963 (sec. 1.42) mentions no secondary stress. Burbiel 2018 (secs. 71-84): no rhythmic secondary stress; a secondary accent arises only in set morphological/syntagmatic configurations - on inflectional suffixes that follow pre-stressing negative -ma or an enclitic particle (main accent stays before -ma: bashlamasỳn 'may he not begin'), on a postposition after its noun, on the last syllable of an adjective after a stressed intensifier (bik), on the last syllable of partial reduplications and of the second member of word-pairs, and on Tatar suffixes attached to recent Russian loans with non-final accent (the suffix accent usually the stronger).

Stress placement is taken from Comrie [2] ('stress in Tatar typically falls on the last syllable of a morphological word, with some exceptions (e.g., loan words from Russian, question words)', p. 3797, sec. 1); the acoustic data place the [L+H*]/[H*] pitch accent on the word-final stressed syllable of sentence-medial subjects and objects ('stressed syllables (which is word-final) of sentence-medial words are marked by rising pitch accents, [L+H*] or [H*]', p. 3797, Abstract; 'focused verbs tend to carry a pitch accent on their final, stressed syllable', p. 3799, sec. 3.4). An optional high tone [Hi] on the first (or second) syllable is analysed as a post-lexical prominence-marking tone, not a pitch accent, 'because it surfaces on an unstressed, non-final syllable of a word' (p. 3797, sec. 1.1), the [Hi] syllable being 'slightly louder than adjacent syllables' (p. 3797, sec. 1.1); it is optional and phrase-edge-bound (p. 3800, sec. 4), so it is not word-level secondary stress.

345.dq: Primary stress falls on the final syllable in a word, with secondary stress on preceding alternate syllables. The initial syllable in a word is never without stress; if a word is polysyllabic, the initial syllable always receives secondary stress, even if this results in adjacent stressed syllables.
345.dloc: MacDonald 1990, A Grammar of Tauya (Mouton), p. 84 — as quoted verbatim in van Urk, 'Clash tolerance' (MIT generals paper) §2.1.2; the Mouton page itself is not in the copy consulted. MacDonald's 1985 UManitoba thesis (sec. 2.5.2, p. 113; also p. 79) carries the same sentence: 'Stress in Tauya is by and large predictable: primary stress falls on the final syllable in a word, with secondary stress on preceding alternate syllables'.
345.prule: Primary stress on the final syllable of the word ('by and large predictable'); exceptions: a few morphemes with unpredictable stress (e.g. /péne/ [pénè] 'star', /séne/ [sénè] 'stone'), and the verbal personal desinences (subject person/number and tense suffixes), which take primary stress on their first syllable, the word's other stresses being adjusted around it (e.g. [yàtéʔa], [yàtámuʔà], [nìyéndè], [nìyándefè]).
345.srule: Secondary stress on alternate syllables preceding the final primary; the initial syllable of every polysyllabic word carries secondary stress even when this yields adjacent stresses ([nònó], [pòtìyafó], [sònòpotìyafó]); around a stressed personal desinence, secondary falls on preceding and following alternate syllables.
345.quote: Stress in Tauya is by and large predictable: primary stress falls on the final syllable in a word, with secondary stress on preceding alternate syllables. The initial syllable in a word is never without stress; if a word is polysyllabic, the initial syllable always has secondary stress. This may result in adjacent stressed syllables. For example: /ʔe/ [ʔé] DEM. 'that (one)' /nono/ [nònó] N. 'child' /fenaʔa/ [fènaʔá] N. 'woman' /ʔʷeiteimo/ [ʔʷèiteimó] N. 'story' /Ø + potiyafo/ [pòtìyafó] N.Inalien. 'his/her hands/arms'

346.sec_rule: Secondary stress on the first of every two syllables before the penultimate primary, counting leftward (("CVCV)n'CVCV: i-"dewa'dewa, i-"hopu"hopu'mai); overridden in reduplications, where secondary stress always falls on the beginning of the reduplicated form (i-"dewade'waya, ina-"bulibu"lili'mai).
346.sec_quote: Secondary stress is applied (counting leftward) to the first of every two syllables prior to the primary-stressed syllable, subject to the rule: ("CVCV)n'CVCV. i-"dewa'dewa it is good; i-"hopu"hopu'mai he/she/it was coming down here. Secondary stress always applies to the beginning of a reduplicated form. This rule overrides the previous rule. i-"dewade'waya he/she/it is doing it; ina-"bulibu"lili'mai he/she/it will be running here

morph.rootq: Schmid 1910 Part II pp.4-5: "The accent presents no difficulties, since it rests almost invariably on the first syllable, if a word consists of two, three or more syllables. Verbs commencing with the syllable cŏm, că, cĕ, as cŏm areshc, că-abeshc, cĕ-nashc, are accented on the second syllable. Exceptions to these two rules will be found accented in the vocabulary." (The rule is stated on the word, but the one systematic exception is the verb-forming/causative prefix syllable cŏm-/că-/cĕ- — identified by Schmid himself on p.27 as a prefix — which is skipped so that accent lands on the root-initial syllable; the word 'root' is not used.)
morph.elicq: Schmid 1910 II p.5: "Exceptions to these two rules will be found accented in the vocabulary." No statement of how accent was determined; Schmid was a missionary who learned the language living among the southern Tehuelche c. 1858-1864 (Fernández Garay 2015:128) and recorded accent per lexical entry in his vocabulary. None of the accessible Fernández Garay articles contains a stress statement (her phonology, 1998:61-108, was not accessible).
morph.stmt: "El tehuelche o aonek'o ʔaʔjen es una lengua aglutinante... Predomina la sufijación sobre la prefijación, y emplea mayoritariamente posposiciones en lugar de preposiciones" (Fernández Garay 2010:38, citing 1998:297-315): person indexes (subject, object, possessor), gender-agreement k-/ʔ-, causative m-, verbaliser kom-/m- and reflexive/middle/reciprocal w-/k- are prefixes (mostly single consonants), while the predicate specifier -š, mood, tense, directionals, number, gender-agreement -e/-n and the nominalisers are suffixes.

tn.quote: Según Suárez (1970, 1973), el tehuelche tiene dos tonos (tono a nivel y tono descendente), que tendrían un bajo nivel de rendimiento funcional. Los únicos pares mínimos ofrecidos afectan a vocales largas: ... já: `el mío’ jà: `yo’ ... Según esto, el tono se usaba en esta lengua para distinguir diferencias gramaticales ... Es decir, no todas las sílabas tehuelche tendrían tono contrastivo. Fernández Garay, en cambio, no encuentra oposición de tonos en tehuelche: esta autora no registra los pares mínimos establecidos por Suárez.
tn.translation: According to Suárez (1970, 1973), Tehuelche has two tones (level tone and falling tone), which would have a low functional load. The only minimal pairs offered involve long vowels: ... já: 'mine' jà: 'I' ... On this account, tone was used in this language to distinguish grammatical differences ... That is, not all Tehuelche syllables would have contrastive tone. Fernández Garay, by contrast, finds no tonal opposition in Tehuelche: this author does not record the minimal pairs established by Suárez.
tn.cite: Viegas Barros, José Pedro. 2015. Proto-Chon: fonología, morfología y léxico. Vol. 1. Tesis de Doctorado, Universidad de Buenos Aires (Facultad de Filosofía y Letras). Ch. 4 sec. 5 'Fenómenos suprasegmentales', pp. 149-163.
tn.note: Schmid 1912 says nothing on tone. Viegas Barros 2015 reports Suárez: 2 tones (level, falling), low functional load, only on stressed syllables; Fernández Garay finds no tonal contrast. Unresolved. Checked against the source (tone consistency check, 2026-09-23): system undetermined -> restricted (p. 156 sec. 5.2.2; p. 163 sec. 5.2.3).

morph.rootq: Stress rule stated on the word: "Word-stress is not significant, falling regularly on the final syllable. Sentence-stress forms part of the suprasegmental accentual system and is accordingly not discussed here, except insofar as it affects allomorphic alternations." (§1.2.2.2, p.139). The grammar separately ties the final syllable to the root: "In general, word-building proceeds by infixation, prefixation and proclisis: suffixation never occurs. The final syllable is therefore in whole or part always the root of the word." (§1.3.1.2, p.141); "a) In final (tonic) syllables, all vowels may occur ... b) In prefinal (atonic) syllables, only short oral vowels may occur" (§1.3.2.2, p.142); and…
morph.elicq: No statement of how stress was determined. Data basis given only as fieldwork: "The author has spent a total of nearly two years in close contact with them, carrying out ethnological and linguistic fieldwork, almost entirely in the Temiar language." (p.129); "Only the segmental phonemes are dealt with here, as no analysis of the intonational system has yet been made." (§1.1, p.130); "Temiar speech-rhythm is 'syllable-timed', i.e. syllabic peaks succeed each other at approximately equal intervals of time." (§1.2.2.1, p.139).
morph.stmt: "In general, word-building proceeds by infixation, prefixation and proclisis: suffixation never occurs. The final syllable is therefore in whole or part always the root of the word." (Benjamin 1976:141, §1.3.1.2) -- Temiar is exclusively pre-root in its bound morphology: proclitic subject pronouns, prepositions/'articles', bar- and -m-, causative tɛr-/bɛr-/-r-, nominaliser (-)n-, and reduplicative aspect/plural copies all precede the root-final (stressed) syllable; in the 74 text tokens = 0 throughout.
